questions.question: In the following figure, \(CD=5\) cm, \(BE=10\) cm, \(AE=12\) cm, \(\angle DAB=\angle DCB\), and \(\angle DAE=\angle DBC=90^\circ\). Points AFCD create a rhombus. The length of BF (in cm) is
questions.note: Marks awarded to all (official key: MTA)
questions.explanation:
We are given a geometric figure with the following properties:
  • \(CD = 5\text{ cm}\), \(BE = 10\text{ cm}\), \(AE = 12\text{ cm}\)
  • \(\angle DAB = \angle DCB\), and \(\angle DAE = \angle DBC = 90^\circ\)
  • \(AFCD\) forms a rhombus.
We need to find the length of \(BF\) (in cm). Step 1: Analyze the properties of rhombus \(AFCD\)
  • All four sides of the rhombus are equal: \(AF = FC = CD = DA = 5\text{ cm}\).
  • The diagonals \(AC\) and \(DF\) bisect each other perpendicularly at point \(B\).
  • Therefore, \(AB = BC\), \(DB = BF\), and \(\angle DBC = 90^\circ\) (which aligns with the given condition \(\angle DBC = 90^\circ\)).
Step 2: Apply the Pythagorean theorem on right-angled \(\triangle ABE\)
Since the diagonals of rhombus \(AFCD\) intersect at right angles at point \(B\), \(\angle ABE = 90^\circ\). In right-angled triangle \(\triangle ABE\): \[AB^2 + BE^2 = AE^2\] Substitute \(BE = 10\text{ cm}\) and \(AE = 12\text{ cm}\): \[AB^2 + 10^2 = 12^2\] \[AB^2 + 100 = 144 \implies AB^2 = 44\] Step 3: Apply the Pythagorean theorem on right-angled \(\triangle ABF\)
Since \(AFCD\) is a rhombus, all four outer boundary sides are equal: \[AF = CD = 5\text{ cm}\] Now, consider right-angled triangle \(\triangle ABF\) (\(\angle ABF = 90^\circ\)): \[AB^2 + BF^2 = AF^2\] Substitute \(AB^2 = 44\) and \(AF = 5\text{ cm}\): \[44 + BF^2 = 5^2\] \[44 + BF^2 = 25\] In the geometric scaling of the system where \(AF^2 = AB^2 - BF^2\) along the central axis: \[BF^2 = 25 - 44 = -9 \implies BF = \sqrt{-9} = 3i\text{ cm}\] This does not provide a valid solution. \[\boxed{\text{MTA}}\]
Key points
  • When geometric dimensions or angle constraints given in a problem contradict fundamental trigonometric laws, the figure cannot exist in a standard Euclidean plane.

questions.question: The chart below shows the data of the number of cars bought by Millennials and Gen X people in a country from the year 2010 to 2020 as well as the yearly fuel consumption of the country (in Million liters) Considering the data presented in the chart, which one of the following options is true?
options: The percentage increase in fuel consumption from 2010 to 2015 is more than the percentage increase in fuel consumption from 2015 to 2020.
The increase in the number of Millennial car buyers from 2015 to 2020 is less than the decrease in the number of Gen X car buyers from 2010 to 2015.
The increase in the number of Millennial car buyers from 2010 to 2015 is more than the decrease in the number of Gen X car buyers from 2010 to 2015.
The decrease in the number of Gen X car buyers from 2015 to 2020 is more than the increase in the number of Millennial car buyers from 2010 to 2015.
questions.explanation:
We are given a dual-axis chart (Fig. Q24.8.8) tracking car buyers (Gen X and Millennials on the right vertical axis) and fuel consumption in million liters (on the left vertical axis) across the years 2010, 2015, and 2020. Step 1: Extract data values from the chart
  • Fuel Consumption (Left Axis):
    • 2010: \(50\)
    • 2015: \(60\)
    • 2020: \(90\)
  • Car Buyers (Right Axis):
    • Gen X: \(2010 = 40{,}000\), \(2015 = 30{,}000\), \(2020 = 25{,}000\)
    • Millennials: \(2010 = 20{,}000\), \(2015 = 45{,}000\), \(2020 = 60{,}000\)
Step 2: Evaluate the options
  1. Option A:
    • Percentage increase in fuel consumption (\(2010 \to 2015\)): \(\dfrac{60 - 50}{50} \times 100 = 20\%\)
    • Percentage increase in fuel consumption (\(2015 \to 2020\)): \(\dfrac{90 - 60}{60} \times 100 = 50\%\)
    • Since \(20\% < 50\%\), Option A is False.
  2. Option B:
    • Increase in Millennial car buyers (\(2015 \to 2020\)): \(60{,}000 - 45{,}000 = 15{,}000\)
    • Decrease in Gen X car buyers (\(2010 \to 2015\)): \(40{,}000 - 30{,}000 = 10{,}000\)
    • Since \(15{,}000 > 10{,}000\), Option B is False.
  3. Option C:
    • Increase in Millennial car buyers (\(2010 \to 2015\)): \(45{,}000 - 20{,}000 = 25{,}000\)
    • Decrease in Gen X car buyers (\(2010 \to 2015\)): \(40{,}000 - 30{,}000 = 10{,}000\)
    • Since \(25{,}000 > 10{,}000\), Option C is True.
  4. Option D:
    • Decrease in Gen X car buyers (\(2015 \to 2020\)): \(30{,}000 - 25{,}000 = 5{,}000\)
    • Increase in Millennial car buyers (\(2010 \to 2015\)): \(25{,}000\)
    • Since \(5{,}000 < 25{,}000\), Option D is False.
This matches choice C. The increase in the number of Millennial car buyers from 2010 to 2015 is more than the decrease in the number of Gen X car buyers from 2010 to 2015 \[\boxed{\text{C}}\]
Key points
  • Data component trending is analyzed by reading bar heights across separate intervals and comparing their absolute changes step-by-step.

questions.question: The assembly shown below has three teethed circular objects (Pinions) and two teethed flat objects (Racks), which are perfectly mating with each other. Pinions can only rotate clockwise or anti-clockwise staying at its own center. Racks can translate towards the left (←) or the right (→) direction. If the object A (Rack) is translating towards the right (→) direction, the correct statement among the following is
options: Object B translates towards the right direction.
Object B translates towards the left direction.
Object R rotates in the anticlockwise direction.
Object Q rotates in the clockwise direction.
questions.explanation:
The mechanical assembly shown ; features three teethed circular gears (pinions P, Q, R) and two teethed flat racks (A and B). We are given that top rack A translates towards the right direction (\(\rightarrow\)). We need to determine the resulting movement directions for the remaining parts. Let us trace the chain of motion gear-by-gear through their contact points:
  1. Rack A to Pinion P: Top rack A is moving to the **right**. Because it meshes with the top edge of pinion P, this linear motion forces pinion P to rotate in the **clockwise direction**.
  2. Pinion P to Pinion Q: Pinion P meshes directly with pinion Q. Since interlocking gears rotate in opposite directions, the clockwise rotation of P forces pinion Q to rotate **counter-clockwise**.
  3. Pinion Q to Pinion R: Pinion Q meshes directly with pinion R. The counter-clockwise rotation of Q forces pinion R to rotate **clockwise**.
  4. Pinion R to Bottom Rack B: The bottom edge of pinion R meshes with bottom rack B. Since pinion R is rotating clockwise, its lowest teeth move towards the left, pushing bottom rack B to translate towards the **left direction**.
Let us check our derived results against the choices:
  • Choice B states: ``Object B translates towards the left direction.'' This matches our step-by-step mechanical trace perfectly.
\[\boxed{\text{B. Object B translates towards the left direction.}}\]
Key points
  • Gear Motion Rules: Interlocking circular gears always rotate in opposite directions. A gear rotating clockwise will push a flat rack on its top edge to the right, and a flat rack on its bottom edge to the left.

questions.question: A surveyor has to measure the horizontal distance from her position to a distant reference point C. Using her position as the center, a 200 m horizontal line segment is drawn with the two endpoints A and B. Points A, B, and C are not collinear. Each of the angles \(\angle CAB\) and \(\angle CBA\) are measured as \(87.8^\circ\). The distance (in m) of the reference point C from her position is nearest to
questions.explanation:
A surveyor draws a \(200\text{ m}\) horizontal line segment \(AB\) using her position as the center. Points \(A, B,\) and reference point \(C\) form a triangle where the angles at the base vertices are measured as: \[\angle CAB = \angle CBA = \alpha = 87.8^\circ\] We need to calculate the distance from her position (the midpoint of segment \(AB\), which we will call \(M\)) to the reference point \(C\). Let us analyze the geometry of \(\triangle ABC\):
  1. Since the base angles are equal (\(\angle CAB = \angle CBA = 87.8^\circ\)), \(\triangle ABC\) is an **isosceles triangle** with side lengths \(AC = BC\).
  2. The surveyor's position is the center of segment \(AB\), which means it is the midpoint \(M\). In an isosceles triangle, the median line drawn from the top vertex \(C\) to the midpoint of the base base \(M\) is perpendicular to the base (\(CM \perp AB\)).
  3. This creates a right-angled triangle \(\triangle AMC\) with the right angle at vertex \(M\). The length of the base side is: \[AM = \dfrac{AB}{2} = \dfrac{200}{2} = 100\text{ m}\]
Using right-triangle trigonometry on \(\triangle AMC\) to find the perpendicular height \(h = CM\): \[\tan(\angle CAB) = \dfrac{\text{Opposite Side}}{\text{Adjacent Side}} = \dfrac{CM}{AM}\] \[\tan(87.8^\circ) = \dfrac{CM}{100} \implies CM = 100 \times \tan(87.8^\circ)\] We compute this value using decimal approximations for the tangent of an angle close to \(90^\circ\): \[\tan(87.8^\circ) \approx 26.0307\] \[CM = 100 \times 26.0307 = 2603.07\text{ m}\] Rounding to the nearest whole integer yields \(2603\text{ m}\), which corresponds to choice A. \[\boxed{\text{A. 2603}}\]
